entries.title: linear-time declaration lookup, metadata interning and union narrowing
entries.body:
A discriminated union the size of typescript-go's node data now compiles in near-linear time, and every program compiles to the same IR as before.

- The attribute pass gathers a function's declarations once, into a name-to-bucket table, instead of re-walking the body on every lookup.
- Round-1 facts no longer allocate a stack-site table the size of the whole program.
- IR metadata is interned through a text-to-index map instead of a linear scan.
- Union narrowing in a switch walks the case's variants beside the remaining ones in one merge pass.
- Operator and equality checks build a union's type name only when they refuse.

Superlinear costs remain in `src/escape.ts`, which allocates a whole-program table per function, and in `src/statements.ts`, where the case-label checks are quadratic in the case count.

Measured: compile time of the generated union program, median of 5, base vs head, with interleaved base/base-copy/head rounds:
- 100 variants: 63 to 43 ms
- 200 variants: 148 to 85 ms
- 400 variants: 540 to 175 ms
- 800 variants: 2699 to 396 ms
- 1600 variants: 13293 to 1085 ms (12.3x)
- self-compile: 2280 to 2248 ms, inside the 4.5% band
Base vs base-copy noise is at most 9%. Per doubling of the variant count, head grows 2.0-2.7x and base 2.3-5.0x. An independent build found all 897 positive cases, all 2315 negative cases and the compiler's own 113 modules byte-identical between base and head.
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: connect nish/net/postgres through a Unix socket
entries.body:
* feat(interop): connect nish/net/postgres through a Unix socket

pgTarget and pgTargetUrl resolve libpq's host and port, or a postgres://
URL, into a PgTarget: a host starting with / or @ is the socket
<host>/.s.PGSQL.<port>, anything else TCP, unchanged. The URL's host, port
and query are percent-decoded; a bad escape or %00 is refused, and so is a
socket path over sun_path, never cut short. The live suite gains a unix
scenario that logs in by peer or trust with a wrong password and reads
over the socket.

Tests: tests/link/std_postgres_unix_target
Tests: tests/postgres/live (unix)

* docs(interop): record and document Unix socket targets for nish/net/postgres

The guide page gains "Connecting over a Unix socket": what pgTarget and
pgTargetUrl take, the 107-byte sun_path limit, and that peer and trust send
no password. The security record adds PG-18 to PG-20 (sun_path, escapes,
host and port splitting) and accepts PG-21 (no socket owner check) and
PG-22 (a socket file taken as a directory, as libpq does). The unit test
gains 3000 seeded URLs pinning that the parser never panics. CI's
postgres-live job mounts the service's socket directory so the unix
scenario runs there under trust.

Tests: tests/link/std_postgres_unix_target, tests/postgres/live (unix)

* refactor(interop): decode postgres URL targets with nish/net/url's urlDecode

pgTargetUrl's own hex decoder is replaced by urlDecode, the audited
percent-decoder in std/net/url.ts. It refuses the same bad escapes and
%00, and also escapes that decode to bytes that are not UTF-8, which is
now PG_TARGET_BAD_ESCAPE.

Tests: tests/link/std_postgres_unix_target

* style(interop): format pgDecoded

* perf(interop): prove the Unix-target URL parser's indexes in range

The performance gate found five bounds checks in pgTargetUrl that the
prover could not drop: loops bounded by the authority's end, which it does
not know lies within the URL. Each loop now also tests the index against
zero and the URL's length, always true, so every check is proven away.

* fix(interop): end a URL's user information at the first @ and refuse a raw NUL anywhere

pgTargetUrl ended the user information at the authority's last `@`, where
libpq ends it at the first, so `postgres://u:p@ss@db/app` named `db` here
and `ss@db` to libpq. A second raw `@` in the authority, or a first `@`
after a `?`, is now refused rather than read either way; an `@` in a
password is written `%40`. A raw NUL byte in any part of the URL, the
parts the parser does not otherwise read included, is refused too, as the
record already claimed.

The guide lists the bracket refusals, IPv6 hosts, that pgTarget does not
percent-decode, and that an empty port or host is refused where libpq takes
it as unset.

Refs: docs/security/postgres.md
Tests: tests/link/std_postgres_unix_target

* test(self): regenerate the postgres bench goldens for the target parser

* test(interop): fuzz connection targets with NUL and non-ASCII bytes

The seeded URLs now include a raw NUL, `é` and its escape, and every
accepted target must hold no NUL in its host or path, so the fuzz backs
PG-19 rather than only "no panic". The security index counts PG-20, fixed
in review.

Tests: tests/link/std_postgres_unix_target

entries.title: time nish break's scripted keys by the clock, not by frames
entries.body:
The two `nish break on a terminal` stage checks failed on main from
a9fcb8d on, and on every PR built on it, with no change to the game or its
terminal code. The relay sent each key once a count of frames had passed,
but the game steps 120 times a second whatever the frame rate, and since
#1100 the rate starts at the best tier and falls under load. At a steady
120 fps the Space meant to start play came three steps before the title's
1 s outro ended, so the `p` after it reached a level still in its intro
and did not pause. After F4 reopened the terminal at 30 fps, the `q` taps
came 333 ms apart, inside KeyState's 700 ms in which a second press of a
key is a repeat, so the game ignored one and never quit.

A scripted key may now carry `afterMs`, the least time since the key
before it. The Space after Enter waits out the outro, each key after a wait
is spaced so it gets a step of its own, and taps of one key are a second
apart. The keys and what each checks are unchanged.
tests: and with all four cores busy)
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: parse and answer HTTP/1.1 requests in a third fewer instructions
entries.body:
The TechEmpower plaintext entry spent more than half its CPU in user space,
and most of that in nish/net/http1 walking the same bytes several times. The
parser now reads each field line once: the scan for the line's end reads
sixteen bytes at a time with one bounds check (a nish:simd load and a
word-at-a-time test for control bytes and DEL), and records whether the line
holds a byte no field value may, so http1FieldLine no longer scans the value
again. A token byte is one shift and mask instead of fourteen comparisons.
The Connection list is walked once for close, keep-alive and upgrade instead
of three times, and a field's four spans are set after one capacity check.
The response writer copies field names, values and the date with one move
each, writes the status, CRLF and ": " with plain stores, and counts digits
without a division loop.

What is refused, and with which status and reason, is unchanged. New checks
put NUL, 0x01, 0x1f, DEL and a bare CR at each byte of a 40-byte value, and
HTAB and obs-text likewise, cutting the stream at every byte at the block
boundaries; the output under Node matches the native one.

The vector load is made in a helper of its own, http1Load16: inside
http1TakeLine's loop the compiler emitted it without its array (invalid IR,
"bitcast i8*  to i8*"), a codegen bug to fix separately.

Also in this change: docs/wp49-async-server.md, the design for async/await
on the server (D1, reversing WP24's refusal for a restricted async, accepted
by the owner), and .claude/plans/wp49-async-server.plan.md, its stages.
metrics: user instructions per plaintext request (callgrind, 32,000 requests 16-deep with TFB's headers, exact): 10,941 before, 7,146 after (-35%)

plaintext 16-deep, server on one core of a shared 4-vCPU VM, wrk on the other three, medians of 3 interleaved rounds of 5 s: 857k / 733k / 694k / 608k req/s at 256 / 1,024 / 4,096 / 16,384 connections, from 589k / 573k / 548k / 451k; uWebSockets.js 607k / 522k / 560k / 552k; noise band 5.7% / 1.1% / 4.0% / 6.6%
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: load a nish:simd vector from an array whose header a loop hoisted
entries.body:
A loop's header hoist collected the arrays its body indexes, takes the
length of, or reads through uncheckedGet/uncheckedSet, but not those a
nish:simd load or store reaches. An inner loop that read only `buf.length`
itself lifted a header with no `data`, and that header shadowed the outer
loop's, so `loadU8x16(buf, i)` inside it took an empty value as its
pointer and emitted `bitcast i8*  to i8*`. The vector access now asks the
hoist for both `len` and `data`, as its bounds check and its load use them.

std/net/http1.ts no longer needs the http1Load16 helper that worked
around it: http1TakeLine calls loadU8x16 directly.
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: read the clock once per serve call for the Date field
entries.body:
HttpDate.current() read Date.now() for every response. Http1Server now
reads the clock once when readable or writable begins a serve call, and
every response written before the flush that ends it carries that reading.
A response written outside a serve call, an answer given later, reads the
clock as it is written; a pinned date wins over both.

Measured: 7,137.1 -> 7,107.8 Ir per request (-29.3, -0.41%), callgrind on
bench/techempower plaintext, 16 pipelined requests per round on one
connection, Ir differenced between 3,200 and 19,200 requests; two runs of
each binary agree within 0.03 Ir per request. Callgrind does not count the
clock syscall valgrind substitutes for the vDSO, so the native saving per
avoided read is larger than this figure.
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: PgCarrier, Postgres queries on the handler's loop
entries.body:
* feat(interop): PgCarrier, Postgres queries on the handler's loop

PgCarrier runs PgPool and PgBatcher queries on an HttpHandler's loop, so a
route handler queries Postgres without blocking its worker. Checkpoint:
the loopback test, seven panic tests and the live suite pass, but placing
the carrier in std/net/postgres.ts breaks the module's deny-every-capability
checks (link/std_postgres_caps and the other std_postgres programs compiled
under --deny), which the security record states as a property. Not ready to
merge until that is resolved.

Tests: tests/link/std_postgres_carrier

* refactor(interop): move PgCarrier into nish/net/postgres-carrier

PgCarrier reads sockets, the clock and the entropy source, and
nish/net/postgres is checked to reach none of them: the std_postgres
programs compile under a policy that denies every capability. The carrier
moves to a module of its own, registered in stdModuleNames, the release
presence gates and std/README.md, and nish/net/postgres goes back to
sans-IO with only the batcher's shed() and readable maxRequests added.

Tests: tests/link/std_postgres_caps, tests/link/std_postgres_carrier

* docs(interop): record PgCarrier's scope, caps and findings, and guide route handlers to it

docs/security/postgres.md now covers std/net/postgres-carrier.ts: its
scope, PG-23 (connect timeout) and PG-24 (a lost execution's batched
requests shed) fixed, PG-25 holding, PG-26 (no per-query deadline)
accepted, its panic sites and its fixed caps. The postgres guide gains
"Querying from a route handler".

Refs: docs/security/postgres.md#findings
Tests: tests/link/std_postgres_carrier

* chore(interop): format nish/net/postgres-carrier

Line breaks only, as biome formats them.

* fix(interop): keep a server's failure past the connect deadline, answer the guide's queries once

The connect deadline no longer overwrites a failure the server already
reported with -110, and a slot's poll interest is changed only when it
differs. The guide's handler example answers each request once, a query
with no row included; PG-23 says how queries waiting on an unreachable
server fail.

* refactor(interop): share the carrier's poll bits and fold its repeated steps

PgCarrier takes its readiness bits from nish/net/http1-server, names the
query an event is about, closes a slot's socket and fills its free stacks
through one helper each, and reads the clock once per connect pass.

* test(self): regenerate the checked goldens for PgBatcher.shed

* test(interop): pin PgCarrier's batching, refusals and close

The carrier's loopback test now counts the batcher's executions on its
stand-in server: three clients' keys go out in one execution and each
client gets its own row or 404, and an execution of three keys lost with
its connection fails all three requests. The stand-in answers a refused
statement with an ErrorResponse, so a plain query's refusal is shown
reaching its own request as PG_CARRIER_ERROR then PG_CARRIER_FAILED with
failure 0, a refused batch failing each of its requests, and the
connection answering the queries after them. close() with a query held by
the server ends that connection while the handler goes on answering.

The live `refused` check now pins ECONNREFUSED (-111), which the old
pattern let the connect timeout's -110 pass as. The panic tests lose their
unused imports, and request_panic's header names what it pins: no event
has named a query yet.

Tests: tests/link/std_postgres_carrier

* docs(interop): name every cause of PgCarrier.attach's panic

attach panics wherever PgPool.register refuses, which is also on a NUL in
the batcher's name or SQL and past 256 statements; the message, the guide
and the security record's panic table now say so. The record's carrier
paragraph describes the new checks and the live suite's current output,
the PostgreSQL row's two Medium findings are counted in the index's Total,
and the class JSDoc sits on PgCarrier rather than on fillFree.

* fix(interop): make PgCarrier.close() final and range-check its watch id

close() is now idempotent and marks the carrier closed: after it, run,
runInt and runText answer PG_CARRIER_FULL and next() answers
PG_CARRIER_NONE, so a carrier used after close() connects nothing on its
closed poll set. Queries in flight at close() get no further event; their
requests are the program's to answer, which the guide and the security
record now say. The constructor checks limits.watch against
HANDLER_MAX_WATCHED before it makes the poll set, so a bad id panics
without leaking a descriptor.

The carrier test now asserts the three clients were taken in one handler
turn, pins the close() refusals, and words its labels to what they check.
The record adds PG-27, a reconnect with no backoff while the server is
down, accepted because the attempts are bounded by the queries waiting,
and states that the flat-arena window excludes the error and reconnect
paths. The live carrier scenario disposes its pool after close().

Refs: docs/security/postgres.md
Tests: tests/link/std_postgres_carrier

entries.title: regions in the runtime (WP46 stage 1)
entries.body:
A fifteenth runtime unit, runtime/runtime-region.c, makes, enters, leaves
and frees a region: an arena of its own behind a 64-bit handle (a 24-bit
slot index and a 40-bit generation). Every call checks the handle first and
panics on a zero handle, a stale or forged one, one made on another thread,
a re-enter, a free while entered and a leave out of order. Entering swaps the
region's arena with the thread's, so the inlined bump allocates into it.

nish_arena_grow reads a thread-local next-chunk size: a region's chunks
start at their first allocation and double, while a thread's own arena keeps
its 64 KiB floor, so 100,000 small regions stay small. The unit is paired in
scripts/build.sh and src/run-cache.ts together, and `--profile wasm` refuses
IR naming @nish_region_ with exit 2, pointing at `--profile wasi`.

The larger slow path shifts LTO's inlining around it: nish_str_from_i32 is
no longer inlined into the map loop, a constant of about 458k instructions a
run. The map-proto-ordered and map-proto-unordered baselines are raised by
that cost; the region path itself runs once per 64 KiB chunk. Mark and
release across a region boundary, the lock held across a region panic and
the unbounded chunk doubling are recorded open for stage 2.
metrics: runtime.c .text 3,453 -> 3,479 (+26) and threads 3,654 -> 3,694 (+40), within their existing ceilings; runtime-region.c 664 (852 threaded); 100,000 regions x 10 rounds resident 38,620 KiB flat; map-proto-ordered +0.181%, map-proto-unordered +0.105% (cachegrind, CI run 41373575079)
